name: Spanish Empire
summary: A global empire built after 1492, spanning the Americas, the Philippines, and parts of Europe and Africa. Its American silver transformed world trade, while conquest and epidemics devastated Indigenous peoples.

knownFor.label: Tercios
knownFor.note: Infantry formations of pikes and firearms that dominated European battlefields.

knownFor.label: Manila galleons
knownFor.note: Ships linking Acapulco and Manila across the Pacific for 250 years.

knownFor.label: Silver “piece of eight”
knownFor.note: Spanish silver coins used in trade around the world, including China.

knownFor.label: Don Quixote
knownFor.note: Cervantes’ novel, often called the first modern novel.

location.value: Centred on Spain, with territories across the Americas (the Caribbean, half of South America, most of Central America and much of North America), the Philippines, parts of Africa, and in Europe (Italy, the Netherlands, for periods).

terrain.value: From the Iberian peninsula across the Atlantic and Pacific, with the Andes and Mexican highlands as cores of colonial wealth.

climate.value: Varied, from temperate Spain to tropical colonies.

resources.value: Silver from Potosí (Bolivia), Zacatecas and Guanajuato (Mexico), gold, sugar, tobacco and cacao.

disasters.value: Epidemics introduced from Europe (smallpox, measles and others), together with conquest, war and forced labour, caused a catastrophic collapse of Indigenous populations in the Americas in the 16th century.
disasters.source: Elliott, Empires of the Atlantic World (2006)

population.value: No total population is given in Wikipedia’s infobox. Indigenous populations in the Americas fell by a very large proportion after contact; estimates vary widely.
population.source: Elliott, Empires of the Atlantic World (2006)

urbanisation.value: Founded many cities in the Americas (Mexico City on the ruins of Tenochtitlan, Lima, Havana, Manila). Potosí became one of the largest cities of the 17th-century world.
urbanisation.source: Kamen, Empire: How Spain Became a World Power (2003)

disease.value: Epidemics devastated Indigenous peoples. The Mexican population is thought to have fallen by most of its pre-conquest size within a century.
disease.source: Elliott, Empires of the Atlantic World (2006)

migration.value: Spanish settlers moved to the Americas. Enslaved Africans were brought by force through the Atlantic slave trade. A mixed (mestizo and mulatto) population grew.
migration.source: Elliott, Empires of the Atlantic World (2006)

economicBase.value: American silver and gold (from Zacatecas, Guanajuato and Potosí) enriched the Crown and paid for wars. Colonial economies relied on mining, plantations and forced Indigenous labour (encomienda, mita).

tradeRoutes.value: Treasure fleets from the Americas to Seville and later Cádiz. The Manila galleons (1565–1815) linked Mexico and China, creating the first truly global trade.

wealth.value: No GDP estimate is given in the sources checked. Its silver inflows contributed to price inflation in Europe (the “price revolution”).
wealth.source: Kamen, Empire: How Spain Became a World Power (2003)

moneyAndTax.value: The silver real and the “Spanish dollar” (from 1598), the world’s first global currency. The Crown defaulted repeatedly on its debts in the 16th–17th centuries.

inequality.value: A colonial caste hierarchy (peninsular Spaniards, American-born Creoles, mestizos, Indigenous peoples, enslaved Africans). Creole resentment of peninsular privilege fed independence movements.

governmentType.value: A composite monarchy (1492–1700), then absolute monarchy under the Bourbons, followed by constitutional monarchy, republics and dictatorship in later Spanish history.

keyRulers.value: The Catholic Monarchs, Isabella and Ferdinand (from 1492). Charles V (1516–1556). Philip II (1556–1598). Philip V (1700–1746, first Bourbon). Charles III (1759–1788, reforms).

succession.value: Dynastic: the Habsburg line ended in 1700 when Charles II died without an heir, leading to the War of the Spanish Succession and the Bourbon Philip V.

institutions.value: The Council of the Indies, viceroyalties (New Spain, Peru, later New Granada and Río de la Plata), the Casa de Contratación, and the Laws of the Indies. The Bourbon Reforms centralised rule in the 18th century.

stability.value: The Iberian Union with Portugal (1580–1640), revolts in Catalonia and Portugal (1640), and Napoleon’s invasion (1808), which triggered the Spanish American wars of independence (1808–1833).

eliteConflict.value: Tensions between the Crown and regional elites, and between peninsular officials and Creole elites in the colonies.

armyAndTech.value: Spanish infantry regiments (tercios), dominant in 16th-century Europe, and the treasure-fleet navy. Conquistadors used steel, horses and firearms, and relied heavily on Indigenous allies.
armyAndTech.source: Kamen, Empire: How Spain Became a World Power (2003)

majorWars.value: Conquest of the Aztec (1519–1521) and Inca (1532–1572) empires. Wars in Europe (Italy, the Dutch Revolt, the Armada of 1588, the Thirty Years’ War). The War of the Spanish Succession. The Spanish–American War (1898).

territoryChange.value: Greatest extent around 1780: about 13.7 million km². Lost most of the mainland Americas by the mid-1820s, and Cuba, Puerto Rico, the Philippines and Guam in 1898. Left Spanish Sahara in 1976.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: Portugal (early), France, England, the Dutch Republic and the Ottomans. Later the United States.

inventions.value: Global navigation and cartography (Magellan–Elcano circumnavigation, 1519–1522), mining technology (mercury amalgamation for silver), and scientific expeditions.

scienceEducation.value: Founded the first universities in the Americas (Santo Domingo 1538, Lima and Mexico City 1551). Scientific expeditions in the 18th century.
scienceEducation.source: Kamen, Empire: How Spain Became a World Power (2003)

openness.value: Strict religious conformity (the Inquisition), but a global exchange of crops, animals and goods (the “Columbian Exchange”).
openness.source: Elliott, Empires of the Atlantic World (2006)

religion.value: Roman Catholicism was the official religion, spread by missionaries across the Americas and the Philippines. Jews were expelled (1492) and Muslims forcibly converted, then expelled (Moriscos, 1609–14).
religion.source: Wikipedia: Spanish Empire (checked 5 Nov 2026) (infobox); Kamen, Empire: How Spain Became a World Power (2003)

languageWriting.value: Spanish (Castilian) became a world language, alongside many Indigenous languages (Quechua, Nahuatl, Maya, Tagalog and others).

artsArchitecture.value: The Spanish Golden Age: Cervantes’ Don Quixote (1605), Velázquez, El Greco, and baroque churches and cities across the Americas.
artsArchitecture.source: Kamen, Empire: How Spain Became a World Power (2003)

socialStructure.value: A hierarchy based on birthplace, ancestry and race. Indigenous forced labour and African slavery.
socialStructure.source: Elliott, Empires of the Atlantic World (2006)

sharedIdentity.value: Catholicism and loyalty to the Crown. Called “the empire on which the sun never sets”.

neighbours.value: Portugal, France, England, the Netherlands, the Ottomans, Indigenous American nations, Ming China (via Manila) and Japan.

ideasReligions.value: Spread Catholicism and the Spanish language. The Columbian Exchange moved maize, potatoes, horses, cattle and diseases between continents.
ideasReligions.source: Elliott, Empires of the Atlantic World (2006)

colonisation.value: One of the largest colonial empires. Its conquests and colonial rule caused enormous suffering and population collapse among Indigenous peoples, a legacy still debated today.
colonisation.source: Elliott, Empires of the Atlantic World (2006)

riseSignals.value: Union of Castile and Aragon, the 1492 voyage of Columbus, conquest of the wealthy Aztec and Inca empires, American silver, and Habsburg inheritance in Europe under Charles V.

peakPeriod.value: Political and military height in the 16th century (Philip II). Greatest territorial extent in the late 18th to early 19th century.

declineSignals.value: Costly European wars, debt defaults, dependence on silver, loss of the Netherlands, rivals’ rising sea power, and Napoleon’s invasion (1808), which broke Crown authority.

outcome.value: Decolonisation. Most of Spanish America became independent by 1833. The last major colonies were lost in 1898, and Spanish Sahara was left in 1976. Spain continues as a European nation-state.

sources.value: Crown and colonial archives (the Archive of the Indies), chronicles, and Indigenous accounts (e.g. the Florentine Codex). Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026 (the article is tagged as needing more citations). See also Elliott (2006) and Kamen (2003).

overallCertainty.value: Good for events and territory. Indigenous population losses and how to weigh disease, violence and forced labour are actively debated.
